definition.text: The community of organisms living all or part of their lives in the soil, and how their feeding links move energy through it.

facts.text: Plant roots feed the web underground by exuding acids, sugars and enzymes into the rhizosphere, and decomposers such as bacteria and fungi end each chain by breaking dead matter into simple nutrients.

Soil organisms range from under 0.1 mm (nematodes) to over 2 mm (earthworms), so small ones are extracted dynamically, for example with a Berlese funnel for arthropods and a Baermann funnel for nematodes.

Soil ecologists found that omnivory is common and that long, complex food chains stay resistant to drying, freezing and fumigation, contradicting May's models that predicted complexity destabilizes webs.
Litter transformers such as isopods enrich their own faecal pellets with microbes and re-eat them, a mutualism called an external rumen that top-down or bottom-up control cannot describe.

definition.text: Bottom-up control is when a resource's density sets its consumer's density; top-down control is when consumers set the abundance of lower trophic levels.

facts.text: Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and resources are the evidence for bottom-up control, as when herbivore and detritivore biomass rises with primary productivity.
A trophic cascade is a top-down effect in which predators change the biomass of organisms at least two links away.
The importance of trophic cascades in terrestrial ecosystems is debated, and cascades may be infrequent because many studies find no top-down effects of predators.

title: Food web representations
article: Soil food web#Types of food webs

definition.text: Food webs are drawn three ways: topological webs, flow webs and interaction webs.

facts.text: Topological webs are non-quantitative maps of which organisms eat which; they are compared by chain length and connectivity.
Flow webs add quantitative carbon or nutrient transfer, built from the biomass of each functional group, usually in kg carbon per hectare, assuming each group is in equilibrium.
Interaction webs show how one group influences another, including indirect effects, such as a predator of root herbivores benefiting the plant roots.
Community matrix models describe each link with Lotka-Volterra equations plus biomass and feeding data, and can show how small changes affect web stability.
